subject: Kemi
title: Air and water
sourceSummary: The composition of air - nitrogen, oxygen and carbon dioxide - the water cycle and its phases, water as a solvent, why ice floats, and the most common air pollutants.

questions.prompt: Which gas is there most of in the air?
questions.opener: It is not the gas we breathe to live - that one comes second.
questions.explanation: Nitrogen (N₂) makes up around 78 per cent of the air, almost four-fifths. Oxygen is of course vital but accounts for only around 21 per cent, and carbon dioxide for less than half a per cent.

questions.prompt: Roughly how much of the air is made up of oxygen?
questions.opener: Just over a fifth of the air is oxygen.
questions.explanation: Oxygen makes up about 21 per cent of the air, just over a fifth. 78 per cent is instead nitrogen's share - easy to mix up if you think air is mostly made of what we breathe.

questions.prompt: What is it called when water vapour in the air cools down and becomes liquid water, for example when clouds and fog form?
questions.opener: It is the opposite of evaporation.
questions.explanation: Condensation is the change from gas to liquid, and it happens when vapour cools down - which is why clouds form high up where it is cold. Evaporation is the opposite change, from liquid to gas, as when the sun warms the sea.

questions.prompt: Why does ice float on water?
questions.opener: Compare how tightly packed the water molecules are in ice compared with in liquid water.
choices: Because ice is colder than water
Because ice always contains air bubbles
Because water expands when it freezes, so the ice ends up with a lower density than the water
Because ice is a completely different substance from water
questions.explanation: When water freezes the molecules arrange themselves in a more open pattern, so the same mass takes up more space - the ice ends up with a lower density and floats. Ice being cold is not enough of an explanation on its own: cold water, after all, does not rise to the surface.

questions.prompt: Why is water called "the universal solvent"?
questions.opener: Think about how many everyday substances actually dissolve in water.
choices: Because water can dissolve absolutely every substance that exists
Because water never reacts with any other substance
Because an unusually large number of substances, such as salt and sugar, dissolve easily in water
questions.explanation: Water dissolves an unusually large number of substances, which is why blood, squash and seawater are all aqueous solutions. But it does not dissolve everything - fat and oil do not dissolve in water but instead sit as a film on top.

questions.prompt: Which gas in the air increases when we burn fossil fuels such as petrol, oil and coal, and strengthens the greenhouse effect?
questions.opener: It is the gas formed when the carbon in the fuel reacts with oxygen.
questions.explanation: Carbon dioxide (CO₂) is formed when the carbon in the fuel burns, and the enhanced greenhouse effect is due to its level increasing. Nitrogen and argon barely take part in the combustion at all, and oxygen is used up rather than increasing.

questions.prompt: The sun warms the surface of the sea. Follow a water molecule through the water cycle all the way back to the sea, naming the phases and phase changes that occur.
questions.opener: Start in the sea as a liquid, and think about what heat and cold each do to the water.
questions.answer: The water evaporates from the sea (liquid to gas), rises, condenses high up in cold air into clouds (gas to liquid), falls as precipitation in the form of rain or snow, and flows via the ground, lakes and rivers back to the sea.
steps: The sun supplies energy to the seawater. The water evaporates, meaning it goes from liquid to gas - it becomes water vapour.
The moist air rises and meets colder air higher up in the atmosphere.
The vapour condenses into small water droplets (gas to liquid) and forms clouds. If it is cold enough, ice crystals form instead.
The droplets grow and fall as precipitation: rain, or snow and hail if it freezes.
The water flows as surface water and groundwater via streams, lakes and rivers back to the sea, and the cycle can begin again. No new water is created - the same water is used over and over again.

questions.prompt: Summarise the composition of air, the properties of water, and the steps of the water cycle.
questions.opener: Take the gases in air with their figures first, then the phases and properties of water.
questions.answer: Composition of air: nitrogen (N₂) about 78% · oxygen (O₂) about 21% · argon just under 1% · carbon dioxide (CO₂) about 0.04% · plus a varying amount of water vapour · Oxygen is needed for breathing and for all combustion · Carbon dioxide is used by plants in photosynthesis and is formed during combustion and respiration · Phases of water: ice (solid), water (liquid), water vapour (gas) · Melting point 0°C, boiling point 100°C at normal air pressure · Phase changes: melting, evaporation (vaporisation), condensation, freezing (solidification) · Ice floats because water expands when it freezes, so the ice has a lower density than the water - this is why lakes freeze from the surface downwards, letting fish survive the winter · Water as a solvent: dissolves an unusually large number of substances, e.g. salt and sugar, but not fat and oil · The water cycle: evaporation from seas and lakes → condensation into clouds → precipitation as rain or snow → the water flows via the ground, lakes and rivers back to the sea · Air pollution: carbon dioxide from fossil fuels strengthens the greenhouse effect, sulphur and nitrogen oxides cause acidification, soot and particles harm the lungs.

questions.prompt: About how much of the air is made up of argon and other noble gases?
questions.opener: It's a very small share compared with nitrogen and oxygen.
questions.explanation: Argon and other noble gases together make up just under 1 percent of the air. 21 percent is oxygen's share and 78 percent is nitrogen's.

questions.prompt: What is it called when water goes from liquid to gas by evaporating from, for example, the sea's surface?
questions.explanation: Evaporation is the change from liquid to gas, for example when the sun heats the sea's surface and water evaporates as water vapour. Condensation is the opposite change, from gas to liquid.

questions.prompt: At what temperature does water have its highest density?
questions.opener: It's actually not at the freezing point, but just above it.
questions.explanation: Water has its highest density at about 4°C. This is why the coldest water in a lake in winter often sits just below the ice, while the slightly warmer 4-degree water sinks to the bottom.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't oil dissolve in water?
questions.opener: Think about how water molecules attract each other strongly, while oil molecules don't in the same way.
choices: Because oil is always too warm
Because the oil molecules and water molecules don't attract each other the way water molecules attract each other
Because water is already saturated with other substances
questions.explanation: Water molecules hold together strongly with each other, while oil molecules don't bond to water in the same way, so oil instead sits as a film on top. This has nothing to do with temperature or saturation.

questions.prompt: Which gases contribute most to the acidification of lakes and forests?
questions.opener: These gases form acids when they react with water in the atmosphere.
questions.explanation: Sulphur and nitrogen oxides from combustion react with water in the air and form sulphuric acid and nitric acid, which fall as acidifying rain. Argon and helium are instead chemically unreactive noble gases that don't contribute to acidification.

questions.prompt: Describe what happens to a water molecule in a rain cloud, all the way until it has become ice on top of a tall mountain.
questions.opener: Think about what's needed for water vapour to become a solid.
questions.answer: The water vapour in the cloud condenses into small water droplets. If it's cold enough up in the cloud, the droplets freeze into ice crystals that fall as snow, and the snow then stays behind as ice on the cold mountain top.
steps: The water vapour in the cloud cools and condenses (gas to liquid) into very small water droplets.
If the air in the cloud is cold enough, the droplets freeze further into ice crystals — this is called freezing (liquid to solid).
The ice crystals grow and eventually fall as snow towards the ground.
The snow lands on the mountain's cold peak, where the temperature stays below freezing, and remains there as ice.

questions.prompt: Which gas is essential for breathing but only makes up about a fifth of the air?
questions.opener: This gas is the one we actually need to breathe, unlike the most common gas in the air.
questions.explanation: Oxygen (O₂) makes up about 21 percent of the air and is the gas cells need to release energy from nutrients. Nitrogen is the most common gas in the air, but it isn't used directly in breathing.
